comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C4-C6, C24-C26. Both OpenEval and all three peer reviewers find the meta-analytic evidence for the MR-GC association convincing and well-supported, citing strong effect sizes, statistical significance, and directional consistency across studies.

Agreement on claims C7-C8, C30-C32 regarding robustness analyses. OpenEval explicitly evaluates the moderator analyses as supported, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings through lack of critique and positive overall assessment of the statistical work.

Strong agreement on uncertainty regarding causal directionality (claims C9, C35-C36, C57). Both OpenEval and Reviewer 2 explicitly note that the correlational meta-analytic data cannot establish whether MR drives GC or vice versa, with Reviewer 2 specifically requesting experimental manipulation studies.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding the broader interpretive framework (claims C37-C39, C64). OpenEval notes this represents theoretical inference requiring validation, while Reviewer 2 challenges the interpretation that GCs function primarily as metabolic signals, emphasizing their broader stress-related effects.

Disagreement on claims C67-C70 regarding dataset characteristics. OpenEval finds these descriptive statistics straightforward and supported, while Reviewers 2 and 3 express concern about limited sample size and potential lab bias, suggesting these represent methodological limitations rather than simple facts.

Agreement on claim C27 regarding model fit statistics. OpenEval explicitly supports this finding, while peer reviewers implicitly accept it through their overall positive assessment of the meta-analytic results without challenging the heterogeneity statistics.
